newsitem.title: POLAND: Over 20 firms get information on Polish oil sector.
newsitem.headline: Over 20 firms get information on Polish oil sector.

text.p: Poland's oil holding Nafta Polska SA has sent information on its privatisation plans to more than 20 international oil firms which have until March 31 to express their interest in the process, Nafta said on Monday.

Nafta, set up to modernise and privatise the country's oil sector, said in a statement an information memorandum, which should not be treated as a formal sale offer, was sent to European, North American and Russian companies and firms from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

"We handed the memorandum to over 20 significant firms of the oil sector...there are European and American concerns among them but also representatives of oil firms from OPEC countries and Russia," it said.
It said investors interested in participating in the privatisation of Poland's two major refineries -- Rafineria Gdanska SA and Petrochemia Plock SA, should express their interest by March 31.
Under the privatisation scheme Nafta Polska, created last year, would offer up to 30 percent of shares in the refineries to potential strategic investors, possibly this year.
The buyers would be allowed to increase their stakes in the refineries to over 50 percent after investing in the modernisation of the companies.

Nafta also said that before the privatisation of the sector Gdansk refinery would take 75 percent of smaller Rafineria Nafty Jedlicze SA and Plock refinery would take 75 percent of Rafineria Trzebinia SA.
Petrochemia Plock had capacity to process 12.6 million tonnes of crude oil per year and Rafineria Gdansk 2.8 million tonnes. Jedlicze has a capacity of 200,000 tonnes and Trzebinia 300,000 tonnes.
Nafta said the prospective investors were expected to guarantee the privatised refineries oil supplies from their own resources.

Investors will also win access to the lucrative state-owned petrol distribution firm CPN SA, which under the plan is to transfer its shares to Nafta and the refineries, but deadlines for allocating CPN's shares to Nafta and refineries have repeatedly been postponed.
CPN owns nearly 1,400 of Poland's 4,700 filling stations.
Under the government programme, Nafta Polska would itself be privatised after several years, most likely through a public share issue, with the state retaining a majority stake.
